items.title: Jim H. Dunbar Jr. Interview, 1959-11-28
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] Well, you know, the thing that really gets me about that band, it's a brass band and the other brass bands have air monitors. But it's like Danny Ruffer said about it.

ctx.x: Well, the one that comes to my mind soonest, or first, is, uh, Young Tuxedos. Uh, see, not one reason for that is I've heard them more, but, um, I've heard several of the other groups. Uh, of course, being, uh, you know, Yankee and from up north and never having a really, you know, heard any records of these groups. Being able to see them and watch, perhaps watch a parade or a funeral or something, is it, if, if, if, if it's nothing else, it's, uh, unique is a overused word. I've been using it too much, but it's…

Well, you know, the thing that really gets me about that band, it's a brass band and the other brass bands have air monitors. But it's like Danny Ruffer said about it. If somebody ever recorded that barrel house brass band and it is really barrel house. Now they can sit there and read those directors and play them pretty straight. You know, you've heard that, about it. No deal. Mm-hmm. But God, they can't really get down to the line, you know. See, it's exciting. Yeah.

Well, you know, I think a white person, we've discussed this many times, but we've discussed the merits, as many people have, of white and Negro musicians. Whether there's any point in discussing that or not, it's not the point here. The point is that one thing certain, I think, about any Negro musician is that he certainly knows legitimacy in a jazz band. This is not the discussion of a degree of musicianship or anything of that sort, but if a band has got it, if it breathes as far, and if it swings, if it is…
